A fourth motion level nobody is offered, and the rule that makes hiding it honest.

## ✨ Added

- **`storm`, a hidden fourth motion level.** Same keyframes, same elements, same tokens: a spring that swings further and takes longer to come to rest. One token block (`:root[data-motion='storm']`) is the whole cost, and that is the language's own rule about intensities paying for itself - a level is a different NUMBER, never a different animation, so a fourth one needs no new machinery. Page 760ms, 34px of travel, `.9` scale on `cubic-bezier(.22, 1.94, .45, 1)` against wild's 420ms, 18px and `.96`; the phone reaches the same shape with `springDamping: 0.34` against 0.68, so the two surfaces overshoot alike rather than merely both overshooting. Asked for by somebody who had just been given the livelier top level and wanted to know whether there was more.
- **The gesture, in `reference/appearance.ts`: `stormTap()`.** Set the motion to the top level, then tap that same option five more times. It is the gesture of pressing a button that is already pressed because you wanted more of it, which is exactly who the level is for, and it is unreachable from any other level on purpose - tapping "off" five times means somebody is annoyed, not curious, and a secret that opens under annoyance is a bug report waiting to be filed.
- **`Motion`, `MOTION_LEVELS`, `DEFAULT_MOTION` and `applyMotion()` join the reference module.** The axis had tokens and a document and no copyable implementation, so every adopting app wrote the attribute-setting half itself - the drift a reference file exists to prevent. `MOTION_LEVELS` is what a picker shows and deliberately excludes `storm`; `applyMotion` accepts it anyway.

## 🎨 Design

- **AN EASTER EGG THAT CHANGES BEHAVIOUR MUST BE SWITCHABLE BACK OFF, AND MUST NOT QUIETLY BECOME A PERMANENT ENTRY IN A SETTINGS LIST.** The rule the fourth level is really here to establish. The first build stored a "found it" flag, so one gesture put a fourth option in the picker for ever after - which turns a secret into a setting somebody has to explain to themselves months later with no memory of how it got there, and which makes a picker's contents depend on history rather than on state.
- **What keeps a hidden option visible is the plain truth about the current state, and nothing else.** It is offered while it is CHOSEN, because a picker that hid the value it is currently showing would be lying about the interface; otherwise only for as long as the settings screen stays open. So `found` lives in the screen's own state and never in storage, while the chosen value persists like any other. The two halves look similar and are not, and storing the wrong one is the mistake above.
- **Validating a stored value and populating a picker are two different questions.** A persisted `storm` is accepted at boot even though no picker offers it, or the gesture would have produced a setting that silently forgets itself on the next reload. An axis with a hidden level is where treating the two as one shows up.
- **A hidden "more animation" switch still sits inside the accessibility gate, not beside it.** `storm` resolves within the same `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)` block as the other three, so a machine whose owner asked the OS for less motion never evaluates a `data-motion` selector at all. That is the one way a secret level could genuinely do harm, and it is closed by where the block sits rather than by a check.
